title: Eventhouse/KQL Hot Cache vs Cold Storage Internals
purpose: Trace an ingested record from the hot cache through the retention-governed cold tier and the OneLake mirror, showing the two independently billed storage tiers, the adaptive-batching decision that governs OneLake writes, and the three-stage capacity throttling ladder that fires under sustained overload.
accessibleSummary: An internals diagram tracing one ingested record through Eventhouse storage. Records land first in the premium-tier hot cache governed by the caching policy, and remain queryable there for fast, low-latency access. In parallel, the full retention window is held in a separate, independently billed standard-tier store governed by the retention policy. If OneLake availability is enabled, an adaptive-batching decision delays the OneLake write until enough data accumulates for optimally sized Parquet files, trading latency for file-size efficiency. A warning node covers the DDL operations blocked while OneLake availability is active. A second warning node describes the three-stage capacity throttling ladder — proactive, reactive, and extreme-reactive — that fires when query and ingestion demand exceeds available capacity.
longDescription: This is an internals diagram over Eventhouse/KQL storage and capacity behaviour, not a data-movement pipeline. It starts at record ingestion and immediately splits into two independently billed storage tiers: a premium cache tier, comparable to ADLS premium, that holds the hot dataset governed by the caching policy, and a standard tier, comparable to ADLS hot, that holds the full retention window governed by the retention policy. Configuring a shorter cache window reduces premium-tier spend without affecting total queryable history, since the standard tier still holds everything within retention. From the standard tier, if OneLake availability is enabled (at the database or individual table level, with optional backfill of existing data), an adaptive-batching mechanism governs when data is actually written to OneLake as Delta/Parquet: it delays writes until enough data accumulates to produce optimally sized files (typically 200-256 MB), defaulting to a maximum delay of up to 3 hours, though the mirroring policy can lower that to as little as 5 minutes at the cost of producing many small files that degrade downstream query performance. The retention policy governs both tiers concurrently — when data ages out, it is deleted from the standard tier and concurrently soft-deleted from the OneLake copy. A warning node captures a specific, sourced trap: while OneLake availability is active on a table, several DDL operations are blocked outright (rename, column type change, row-level security, delete/purge), and enabling it back after a temporary disable triggers a full historic backfill rather than an incremental catch-up. A second warning node describes the escalating three-stage throttling ladder Eventhouse applies under capacity pressure — proactive (queries slow, ingestion unaffected), reactive (both paused, no data lost), and extreme-reactive (both paused with a real risk of data loss after a holding period) — which is the operational consequence of undersizing capacity against the ingestion and query load these two storage tiers actually sustain.

nodes.label: Record ingested into KQL database
nodes.summary: An event record arrives and is organized by arrival time for fast, indexed querying.
nodes.detail: Eventhouses automatically organize ingested records by arrival time, enabling fast, indexed queries over structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data at any scale. From this point, the same logical record exists in two independently governed storage tiers, described in the next two nodes.
nodes.whyItMatters: The arrival-time organization is what makes both the hot cache and the cold standard tier fast to query without a separate indexing step — it is foundational to everything downstream in this diagram.

evidence.note: Eventhouses automatically organize ingested records by arrival time, enabling fast, indexed queries over structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data at any scale. Data stored in an Eventhouse is also mirrored to OneLake as a single logical copy for use by other Fabric experiences.

inputs: A streaming or batch record arriving via Eventstream or direct ingestion into a KQL database table
processing: Record is indexed and organized by arrival time
Record becomes queryable via native KQL and the T-SQL analytics endpoint
Record is routed into the caching-policy hot tier and the retention-policy standard tier concurrently
outputs: A queryable record, present in both the hot cache and the durable standard-tier store
drill.example: A telemetry event from a fleet-tracking Eventstream lands in a KQL database table and is immediately queryable via KQL within seconds, indexed by its arrival timestamp alongside millions of other records from the same ingestion window.
controls: Ingestion source and format (Eventstream, direct SDK/API ingestion, batch)
failureModes: Assuming query latency is uniform regardless of how old the queried data is — it is not, because hot and cold tiers behave differently (see the next two nodes)

nodes.label: Hot cache tier (caching policy)
nodes.summary: Premium-tier storage holding the hot dataset for fast queries, governed by the caching policy.
nodes.detail: KQL database storage is split into two independently billed tiers: a premium cache tier, comparable to ADLS premium, that holds the hot dataset governed by the caching policy. Configuring a shorter cache window reduces premium-tier spend without affecting total queryable history, because the standard tier separately holds the full retention window regardless of the cache window's length.
nodes.whyItMatters: This tier is the actual latency lever: queries against data inside the cache window run against premium storage, while queries reaching further back fall outside it — the cache window is a cost/performance dial, not a data-loss risk, since the standard tier still holds everything within retention.

evidence.note: KQL database storage is split into two independently billed tiers: a premium cache tier (comparable to ADLS premium) that holds the hot dataset governed by the caching policy, and a standard tier (comparable to ADLS hot) that holds the full retention window governed by the retention policy. Configuring a shorter cache window reduces premium-tier spend without affecting total queryable history.

inputs: Recently ingested records, within the configured caching-policy window
processing: Data within the cache window is kept resident in premium-tier storage
Queries against this window read directly from premium storage for lower latency
outputs: Fast query response for recent data, billed at premium-tier rates for the cache window's size
drill.example: A dashboard querying the last 24 hours of IoT telemetry with a 48-hour caching policy always hits premium-tier storage, giving consistently fast response times regardless of how much older history the table also retains.
controls: Caching policy window length, set independently of the retention policy
failureModes: Setting an unnecessarily long cache window and paying premium-tier rates for data that queries rarely touch
Assuming shortening the cache window deletes data — it only moves the boundary of what's held at premium-tier speed, not what's retained

nodes.label: Cold standard tier (retention policy)
nodes.summary: Standard-tier storage holding the full retention window, governed by the retention policy.
nodes.detail: The standard tier, comparable to ADLS hot, holds the full retention window governed by the retention policy, independently billed from the premium cache tier. The retention policy also governs the OneLake copy concurrently: data aged out of the KQL database is concurrently soft-deleted from OneLake.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the tier that actually determines how far back a query can reach at all — the retention policy, not the caching policy, is the real data-lifecycle control, and it has a direct, concurrent effect on the separate OneLake copy.

evidence.note: KQL database storage is split into two independently billed tiers: a premium cache tier and a standard tier (comparable to ADLS hot) that holds the full retention window governed by the retention policy.
The KQL retention policy also governs the OneLake copy: data aged out of the KQL database is concurrently soft-deleted from OneLake.

inputs: All ingested records within the configured retention window, regardless of cache-window membership
processing: Data is held in standard-tier storage for the full retention period
When data ages past the retention window, it is deleted from the standard tier and concurrently soft-deleted from OneLake if OneLake availability is enabled
outputs: The full queryable history within retention, at standard-tier cost, plus a synchronized deletion signal to the OneLake mirror
drill.example: A table with a 2-year retention policy and a 48-hour cache window keeps two years of history queryable (at standard-tier latency beyond 48 hours) and automatically soft-deletes both the KQL copy and the OneLake copy of any record older than two years.
controls: Retention policy window, set per table or database
failureModes: Assuming the OneLake copy persists independently of KQL retention — it does not; the same retention policy prunes both concurrently
Setting retention shorter than a downstream OneLake consumer (e.g. a Lakehouse job) expects, silently losing history that consumer assumed was durable

nodes.label: OneLake availability enabled?
nodes.summary: Whether the table's data is also exposed as Delta in OneLake, at the database or table level.
nodes.detail: OneLake availability for a KQL database can be enabled at either the database level (covering all current and future tables, with optional backfill of existing data) or at the individual table level. Enabling it exposes KQL table data in Delta Lake format, making it directly queryable by other Fabric engines — including Power BI Direct Lake mode, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark notebooks — without any data movement or copy, and at no additional storage charge beyond the standard OneLake storage tier already billed.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the fork that determines whether KQL data becomes a first-class OneLake citizen usable by the rest of Fabric, or stays confined to KQL/T-SQL query surfaces — a decision with real downstream architectural consequences.

evidence.note: OneLake availability for a KQL database can be enabled at either the database level (covering all current and future tables, with optional backfill of existing data) or at the individual table level.

Enabling OneLake availability exposes KQL table data in Delta Lake format, making it directly queryable by other Fabric engines — including Power BI Direct Lake mode, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark notebooks — without any data movement or copy. There is no additional storage charge for the OneLake copy beyond the standard OneLake storage tier already billed.

inputs: A KQL database or individual table, with a decision on whether cross-engine access to its data is needed
processing: If enabled at database level: all current and future tables get OneLake availability, with optional backfill for existing data
If enabled at table level: only that specific table is exposed
If left disabled: data stays queryable only via native KQL and the T-SQL analytics endpoint
outputs: Either a Delta-format OneLake mirror usable by Direct Lake, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark, or KQL-only access with no OneLake footprint
drill.example: A team enables OneLake availability at the database level with backfill for a telemetry KQL database so a Direct Lake semantic model can report on it directly, at no incremental OneLake storage cost beyond what's already billed.
controls: Whether to backfill existing data or start availability from the point of enablement forward
failureModes: Enabling database-level availability without realizing it applies to all future tables too, exposing data that wasn't meant to be OneLake-visible
Not requesting backfill, and assuming historical data is available in OneLake when only new data going forward actually is

nodes.label: Adaptive batching to OneLake
nodes.summary: OneLake writes are delayed until enough data accumulates for optimally sized Parquet files.
nodes.detail: When OneLake availability is active, an adaptive batching mechanism delays writes to OneLake until enough data accumulates to produce optimally-sized Parquet files (typically 200-256 MB). The default maximum delay is up to 3 hours; it can be lowered to as little as 5 minutes via the mirroring policy, though smaller delays risk producing many small files that degrade downstream query performance.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a real latency-vs-file-efficiency tradeoff that architects must consciously set, not a fixed platform constant — the default 3-hour ceiling means OneLake-side freshness is meaningfully behind KQL-native freshness unless the mirroring policy is explicitly tuned tighter, and tuning it tighter has its own downstream query-performance cost.

evidence.note: When OneLake availability is active, an adaptive batching mechanism delays writes to OneLake until enough data accumulates to produce optimally-sized Parquet files (typically 200-256 MB). The default maximum delay is up to 3 hours; it can be lowered to as little as 5 minutes via the mirroring policy, though smaller delays risk producing many small files that degrade downstream query performance.

inputs: Newly ingested records in a table with OneLake availability enabled
The configured mirroring policy delay (default up to 3 hours, tunable down to 5 minutes)
processing: Accumulate incoming records until either the target file size (200-256 MB) is reached or the maximum delay elapses
Write the accumulated batch to OneLake as a Delta/Parquet file
outputs: Delta-format files in OneLake, sized for efficient downstream query performance, at some latency behind KQL-native freshness
drill.example: A high-volume table hits the 200-256 MB file-size target every 20 minutes during peak ingestion, so OneLake freshness tracks close to real time; the same table during a quiet period waits the full 3-hour default before a smaller batch is flushed.
controls: Mirroring policy delay, tunable from the 3-hour default down to 5 minutes
failureModes: Tuning the delay down to 5 minutes for freshness without accounting for the resulting small-file query-performance cost downstream
Assuming OneLake-side data is as fresh as KQL-native queries, when it can lag by up to 3 hours under the default policy

nodes.label: Trap: blocked DDL while OneLake-available
nodes.summary: Rename, type change, row-level security, and delete/purge are blocked while OneLake availability is active.
nodes.detail: While OneLake availability is enabled on a table, certain DDL operations are blocked: renaming the table, changing a column's data type, applying row-level security, and deleting or purging rows. These operations require temporarily disabling OneLake availability; re-enabling it triggers a full historic backfill.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a real operational trap for schema evolution: a team that enables OneLake availability early and later needs to rename a column or apply row-level security discovers the operation is blocked, and the fix (disable, change, re-enable) forces a full historic re-backfill rather than an incremental change.

evidence.note: While OneLake availability is enabled on a table, certain DDL operations are blocked: renaming the table, changing a column's data type, applying row-level security, and deleting or purging rows. These operations require temporarily disabling OneLake availability; re-enabling it triggers a full historic backfill.

inputs: A table with OneLake availability enabled
A required DDL change: rename, column type change, row-level security, or delete/purge
processing: Attempting the DDL directly fails while OneLake availability is active
Disable OneLake availability on the table
Re-enable OneLake availability, which triggers a full historic backfill rather than an incremental resync
outputs: The DDL change applied, but at the cost of a full re-backfill of OneLake data for that table
drill.example: A compliance requirement to apply row-level security to a customer telemetry table, already OneLake-available for six months of history, forces a disable/apply/re-enable cycle that re-backfills the entire six months into OneLake rather than just applying the new policy incrementally.
controls: Plan schema and security requirements (renames, type changes, row-level security) before enabling OneLake availability, not after
Budget for a full backfill window when a blocked DDL operation is unavoidable on an already-available table
failureModes: Discovering the DDL block only when an urgent schema or security change is needed, with no backfill window planned
Repeated disable/re-enable cycles each re-triggering a full backfill, compounding cost and delay

nodes.label: Three-stage capacity throttling ladder
nodes.summary: Proactive, reactive, and extreme-reactive throttling stages fire as capacity pressure escalates.
nodes.detail: When query demand exceeds capacity, an Eventhouse applies throttling in three escalating stages: proactive (queries slowed, ingestion unaffected), reactive (both queries and ingestion paused but no data lost), and extreme-reactive (ingestion and queries paused with a risk of data loss after a holding period). Workspace-level surge protection lets capacity administrators cap each workspace's share of total CU consumption as a percentage over a rolling 24-hour window, and a workspace breaching its threshold is automatically blocked from accepting new operations, though mission-critical workspaces can be exempted.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the concrete operational consequence of undersizing capacity against the ingestion and query load the hot and cold tiers above actually sustain — and the escalation is not symmetric: the first two stages are recoverable with no data loss, but the third genuinely risks losing data after a holding period.

evidence.note: When query demand exceeds capacity, an Eventhouse applies throttling in three escalating stages: proactive (queries slowed, ingestion unaffected), reactive (both queries and ingestion paused but no data lost), and extreme-reactive (ingestion and queries paused with a risk of data loss after a holding period).

Workspace-level surge protection allows capacity administrators to cap each workspace's share of total CU consumption as a percentage over a rolling 24-hour window. When a workspace breaches its threshold it is automatically blocked from accepting new operations; high-priority workspaces can be designated as mission-critical to exempt them from these rules.

inputs: Sustained query and/or ingestion demand approaching or exceeding available capacity
processing: Stage 1 (proactive): queries slow down, ingestion continues unaffected
Stage 2 (reactive): both queries and ingestion pause, but no data is lost while paused
Stage 3 (extreme-reactive): both remain paused, and data loss becomes a real risk after a holding period
outputs: Either recovery as demand subsides at stage 1 or 2, or actual data loss if stage 3 is sustained past the holding period
drill.example: A capacity undersized for a sudden 5x ingestion spike from a new Eventstream source first slows queries (stage 1); if the spike continues and capacity isn't increased, ingestion itself pauses (stage 2); left unaddressed past the holding period, incoming events begin to be dropped (stage 3).
controls: Capacity sizing sufficient for peak, not average, ingestion and query load
Workspace-level surge protection to cap runaway consumption before it escalates the whole capacity toward stage 3
Mission-critical workspace exemption for workloads that must never be throttled
failureModes: Sizing capacity for average load and getting blindsided by a burst that pushes straight through proactive into reactive throttling
Assuming all three stages are equally safe — extreme-reactive is the only one that risks real data loss, and it is reached only after sustained pressure past the holding period

edges.label: check whether OneLake availability is configured
OneLake write load contributes to capacity pressure

walkthrough.title: Start: one record, two storage tiers
walkthrough.explanation: An ingested record is organized by arrival time and immediately becomes part of two independently governed, independently billed storage tiers.

walkthrough.title: Hot: premium-tier cache for fast queries
walkthrough.explanation: The caching policy window keeps recent data resident in premium storage — a cost/performance dial, not a retention control.

walkthrough.title: Cold: standard-tier store for the full retention window
walkthrough.explanation: The retention policy is the real data-lifecycle control, and it governs both the KQL standard tier and the OneLake copy concurrently.

walkthrough.title: The fork: is this table OneLake-visible?
walkthrough.explanation: Enabling OneLake availability, at the database or table level, exposes KQL data as Delta to every other Fabric engine at no extra storage cost — but it isn't free of consequences, covered in the next two nodes.

walkthrough.title: Adaptive batching trades latency for file efficiency
walkthrough.explanation: OneLake writes wait for an optimal file size or a maximum delay (3 hours by default, tunable to 5 minutes) — freshness and small-file query cost pull in opposite directions.

walkthrough.title: Warning: OneLake availability blocks some DDL
walkthrough.explanation: Rename, type change, row-level security, and delete/purge are blocked while enabled — the fix forces a full historic backfill, not an incremental change.

walkthrough.title: Warning: capacity pressure escalates in three stages
walkthrough.explanation: Proactive and reactive throttling are recoverable with no data loss; extreme-reactive genuinely risks losing data after a holding period — the real cost of undersizing capacity for what these tiers sustain.
